items.micro_skill: new average after one value joins
items.stem: The average age of the 7 teachers in the barangay hall is 21 years. One more person, with 29 years, joins them. What is the new average age?

reveal.terms: "Average" means share equally.
reveal.shortcut: The new person is 29 − 21 = 8 above the old average. Share that among all 8 people: 8 ÷ 8 = 1. Add it: 21 + 1 = 22.

why_wrong.o1: This averages 21 and 29 only, treating the 7 old members as one person.
why_wrong.o3: This shares the extra 8 years among 7 people. After the new person joins there are 8.
why_wrong.o4: This is the total of all 8 values. It stops before dividing by 8.

method_steps.1_asked: The new average age of all 8 people.
method_steps.2_givens: 7 people averaging 21; one more with 29
method_steps.3_method: Average = total ÷ number of people. Find the old total, add the newcomer, divide by the new count.
method_steps.4_why: You cannot average the old average with the newcomer: the old average stands for many people.
method_steps.5_solve_by_hand: Old total = 7 × 21 = 147. New total = 147 + 29 = 176. New average = 176 ÷ 8 = 22.
method_steps.7_distractors: 25 years: This averages 21 and 29 only, treating the 7 old members as one person. 22.14 years: This shares the extra 8 years among 7 people. After the new person joins there are 8. 176 years: This is the total of all 8 values. It stops before dividing by 8.
method_steps.8_shortcut: The newcomer is 8 above the average; spread that over 8 people: 21 + 8 ÷ 8 = 22.

items.micro_skill: compare rational numbers with unequal denominators
items.stem: A health worker filled four identical containers to 4/7, 5/9, 7/12, and 3/5 of their capacity. What fraction is the fullest?

reveal.shortcut: Compare each with 3/5 using cross multiplication. For 7/12, compare 7 × 5 = 35 with 3 × 12 = 36; 3/5 wins. The others are smaller too.

why_wrong.o4: 5/9 is less than 3/5: cross-products are 25 and 27, so the second fraction is larger.

method_steps.4_why: All four are just over 1/2, so the size of the excess decides.
method_steps.5_solve_by_hand: Excess over 1/2: 4/7 → 1/14; 5/9 → 1/18; 7/12 → 1/12; 3/5 → 1/10. The largest excess is 1/10, so 3/5 is fullest.

method_steps.8_shortcut: Fraction minus 1/2 = (2 × top − bottom) ÷ (2 × bottom).

items.micro_skill: adjust hours when the number of workers changes
items.stem: Eight trained packers can finish an order in 15 hours. If 12 equally fast packers handle the same order, how many hours will it take?

reveal.terms: For the same job, more equally fast workers need fewer hours.
reveal.shortcut: Total work is 8 × 15 = 120 packer-hours. Divide by 12 packers: 120 ÷ 12 = 10 hours.
reveal.why_correct: 12 packers × 10 hours = 120 packer-hours, the same work as 8 × 15.

why_wrong.o1: 22 1/2 hours increases the time when more packers are added; for the same work, time should decrease.
why_wrong.o3: 15 hours assumes the larger team works no faster than the original eight.
why_wrong.o4: 11 hours subtracts the four additional packers from the hours, mixing different units.

method_steps.3_method: Total work in packer-hours, then divide.

items.micro_skill: add job fractions completed per hour
items.stem: One pump empties a pond in 8 hours. Another pump can empty the same pond in 12 hours. If both operate together from the start, how long will they take?

reveal.terms: Two pumps working together add the parts of a pond they empty each hour.
reveal.shortcut: In one hour they empty 1/8 + 1/12 = 5/24 of the pond. Total hours = 24/5 = 4 4/5 hours.
reveal.why_correct: 4 4/5 hours × 5/24 pond per hour = one whole pond. Both pumps finish faster than either pump alone.

why_wrong.o1: 10 hours averages the completion times and is slower than the faster pump alone.
why_wrong.o2: 6 hours assumes two pumps each work at the slower pump’s rate; their actual rates differ.
why_wrong.o3: 20 hours adds the individual completion times instead of adding their hourly work rates.

method_steps.1_asked: Time for both pumps together.
method_steps.2_givens: 8 hours and 12 hours alone
method_steps.3_method: Add the hourly fractions, then flip.
method_steps.4_why: Pumps working together add their rates, not their times.
method_steps.7_distractors: 10 hours: 10 hours averages the completion times and is slower than the faster pump alone. 6 hours: 6 hours assumes two pumps each work at the slower pump’s rate; their actual rates differ. 20 hours: 20 hours adds the individual completion times instead of adding their hourly work rates.

items.micro_skill: convert mixed hours to speed and trip time
items.stem: A provincial bus covers 72 kilometers in 1 1/2 hours at a steady speed. How many hours will it need to travel 120 kilometers at the same speed?

reveal.terms: Speed equals distance divided by time; time equals distance divided by speed.
reveal.shortcut: Speed: 72 ÷ 1 1/2 = 48 km/h. For 120 km, time is 120 ÷ 48 = 2 1/2 hours.
reveal.why_correct: 48 km/h × 2 1/2 hours = 120 km, matching the distance.

why_wrong.o2: 0.9 hour reverses the distance ratio, making a longer trip take less time.
why_wrong.o3: 48 hours mistakes the bus speed, 48 kilometers per hour, for a travel time.
why_wrong.o4: 1 1/2 hours repeats the time for the shorter 72-kilometer trip without increasing the time for the longer 120-kilometer trip.

method_steps.1_asked: Hours for 120 km.
method_steps.2_givens: 72 km in 1 1/2 h
method_steps.3_method: Find the speed, then time = distance ÷ speed.
method_steps.4_why: Same speed throughout.
method_steps.7_distractors: 0.9 hours: 0.9 hour reverses the distance ratio, making a longer trip take less time. 48 hours: 48 hours mistakes the bus speed, 48 kilometers per hour, for a travel time. 1 1/2 hours: 1 1/2 hours repeats the time for the shorter 72-kilometer trip without increasing the time for the longer 120-kilometer trip.

items.micro_skill: use total distance divided by total time
items.stem: A delivery van travels 50 kilometers at 50 km/h, then another 50 kilometers at 25 km/h. What is the average speed for the entire 100-kilometer trip?

reveal.terms: Average speed is total distance divided by total travel time.
reveal.shortcut: First 50 km takes 1 hour. Second 50 km takes 2 hours. Total: 100 km in 3 hours, so 100 ÷ 3 = 33 1/3 km/h.
reveal.why_correct: At 33 1/3 km/h, three hours cover 100 km. The slower portion lowers the overall speed.

why_wrong.o1: 100 km/h repeats the total distance as if it were a speed.
why_wrong.o3: 37 1/2 km/h takes the simple average of two speeds even though the slow segment takes longer.
why_wrong.o4: 50 km/h is only the speed on the first segment.

method_steps.1_asked: Average speed for the whole trip.
method_steps.2_givens: 50 km at 50 km/h; 50 km at 25 km/h
method_steps.3_method: Average speed = total distance ÷ total time.
method_steps.4_why: Do not average the speeds: more time was spent at the slower speed.
method_steps.5_solve_by_hand: Times: 1 h and 2 h. 100 km ÷ 3 h = 33 1/3 km/h.
method_steps.7_distractors: 100 km/h: 100 km/h repeats the total distance as if it were a speed. 37 1/2 km/h: 37 1/2 km/h takes the simple average of two speeds even though the slow segment takes longer. 50 km/h: 50 km/h is only the speed on the first segment.
method_steps.8_shortcut: Equal distances: 2ab ÷ (a + b) = 2500 ÷ 75 = 33 1/3.

why_wrong.o3: 20 stools is the red share of four parts, not the blue share of seven.

method_steps.3_method: Total parts, one part, then the share.

method_steps.7_distractors: 11 stools: 11 stools counts the total number of ratio parts as if each part were one stool. 20 stools: 20 stools is the red share of four parts, not the blue share of seven. 5 stools: 5 stools is the value of one part before multiplying by seven.

why_wrong.o1: 78 sacks adds the coffee count to the cacao count, giving the combined total.
why_wrong.o3: 30 sacks simply repeats the coffee count, assuming equal counts instead of the 5-to-8 ratio.
why_wrong.o4: 6 sacks is one ratio part; cacao requires eight such parts.

method_steps.1_asked: The number of cacao sacks.

items.micro_skill: identify the gap between two ratio shares
items.stem: Two barangay teams have recycling crates in the ratio 4 : 5. Together they have 36 crates. Without removing any crates from the larger team, how many must be added to the smaller team to match it?

reveal.terms: Equalizing two shares means adding the difference to the smaller share.
reveal.shortcut: The ratio has 4 + 5 = 9 parts. One part = 36 ÷ 9 = 4 crates. The shares differ by one part, so add 4.
reveal.why_correct: The smaller team starts with 16 crates. Adding 4 gives 20, matching the larger team.

why_wrong.o1: 20 crates is the larger team’s existing count, not the difference.
why_wrong.o2: 36 crates repeats the combined amount rather than finding the one-part gap.
why_wrong.o3: 16 crates is what the smaller team already owns, not how many it needs.

method_steps.1_asked: Crates to add to the smaller team.
method_steps.2_givens: 4 : 5; 36 crates
method_steps.3_method: Find each team's count, then the gap.
method_steps.4_why: Equalizing means adding the difference to the smaller team.
method_steps.5_solve_by_hand: 9 parts = 36, so 1 part = 4. Teams: 16 and 20. Add 20 − 16 = 4.
method_steps.7_distractors: 20 crates: 20 crates is the larger team’s existing count, not the difference. 36 crates: 36 crates repeats the combined amount rather than finding the one-part gap. 16 crates: 16 crates is what the smaller team already owns, not how many it needs.
method_steps.8_shortcut: The gap is 1 part = 4.
